The `make_sentinel` function defines a `Sentinel` class with a `__bool__` method that always returns `True`. This means that any sentinel object created with `make_sentinel` will evaluate to `True` in a boolean context. The test `test_sentinel_falsiness` is failing because it expects `NOT_SET` to be falsy, but the `__bool__` method makes it truthy. To fix this, we need to modify the `__bool__` method to return `False` for the sentinel object. Let's make this change and verify that the test passes.

   335	class AtomicSaver:
   336	    """``AtomicSaver`` is a configurable `context manager`_ that provides

   338	    no exceptions are raised within the context manager's block. These
   339	    "part files" are created in the same directory as the destination
   340	    path to ensure atomic move operations (i.e., no cross-filesystem
   341	    moves occur).
   342	
   343	    Args:
   344	        dest_path (str): The path where the completed file will be
   345	            written.
   346	        overwrite (bool): Whether to overwrite the destination file if
   347	            it exists at completion time. Defaults to ``True``.
   348	        file_perms (int): Integer representation of file permissions
   349	            for the newly-created file. Defaults are, when the
   350	            destination path already exists, to copy the permissions
   351	            from the previous file, or if the file did not exist, to
   352	            respect the user's configured `umask`_, usually resulting
   353	            in octal 0644 or 0664.
   354	        text_mode (bool): Whether to open the destination file in text
   355	            mode (i.e., ``'w'`` not ``'wb'``). Defaults to ``False`` (``wb``).
   356	        part_file (str): Name of the temporary *part_file*. Defaults
   357	            to *dest_path* + ``.part``. Note that this argument is
   358	            just the filename, and not the full path of the part
   359	            file. To guarantee atomic saves, part files are always
   360	            created in the same directory as the destination path.
   361	        overwrite_part (bool): Whether to overwrite the *part_file*,
   362	            should it exist at setup time. Defaults to ``False``,
   363	            which results in an :exc:`OSError` being raised on
   364	            pre-existing part files. Be careful of setting this to
   365	            ``True`` in situations when multiple threads or processes
   366	            could be writing to the same part file.
   367	        rm_part_on_exc (bool): Remove *part_file* on exception cases.
   368	            Defaults to ``True``, but ``False`` can be useful for
   369	            recovery in some cases. Note that resumption is not
   370	            automatic and by default an :exc:`OSError` is raised if
   371	            the *part_file* exists.
   372	
   373	    Practically, the AtomicSaver serves a few purposes:

   377	      * Providing a reasonable guarantee that a part file only has one
   378	        writer at a time.

   495	def complement(wrapped):
   496	    """Given a :class:`set`, convert it to a **complement set**.
   497	
   498	    Whereas a :class:`set` keeps track of what it contains, a
   499	    `complement set
   500	    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory)>`_ keeps
   501	    track of what it does *not* contain. For example, look what
   502	    happens when we intersect a normal set with a complement set::
   503	
   504	    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
   505	    [0, 1, 4]
   506	
   507	    We get the everything in the left that wasn't in the right,
   508	    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting
   509	    a normal set.
   510	
   511	    Args:
   512	        wrapped (set): A set or any other iterable which should be
   513	           turned into a complement set.
   514	
   515	    All set methods and operators are supported by complement sets,
   516	    between other :func:`complement`-wrapped sets and/or regular
   517	    :class:`set` objects.
   518	
   519	    Because a complement set only tracks what elements are *not* in
   520	    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
   521	    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
   522	    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by
   523	    complementing it again:
   524	
   525	    >>> s = set(range(5))
   526	    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
   527	    True
   528	
   529	    .. note::
   530	
   531	       An empty complement set corresponds to the concept of a
   532	       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
   533	       from mathematics.
   534	
   535	    Complement sets by example
   536	    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   537	
   538	    Many uses of sets can be expressed more simply by using a
   539	    complement. Rather than trying to work out in your head the proper
   540	    way to invert an expression, you can just throw a complement on
   541	    the set. Consider this example of a name filter::
   542	
   543	        >>> class NamesFilter(object):
   544	        ...    def __init__(self, allowed):
   545	        ...        self._allowed = allowed
   546	        ...
   547	        ...    def filter(self, names):
   548	        ...        return [name for name in names if name in self._allowed]
   549	        >>> NamesFilter(set(['alice', 'bob'])).filter(['alice', 'bob', 'carol'])
   550	        ['alice', 'bob']
   551	
   552	    What if we want to just express "let all the names through"?
   553	
   554	    We could try to enumerate all of the expected names::
   555	
   556	       ``NamesFilter({'alice', 'bob', 'carol'})``
   557	
   558	    But this is very brittle -- what if at some point over this
   559	    object is changed to filter ``['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dan']``?
   560	
   561	    Even worse, what about the poor programmer who next works
   562	    on this piece of code?  They cannot tell whether the purpose
   563	    of the large allowed set was "allow everything", or if 'dan'
   564	    was excluded for some subtle reason.
   565	
   566	    A complement set lets the programmer intention be expressed
   567	    succinctly and directly::
   568	
   569	       NamesFilter(complement(set()))
   570	
   571	    Not only is this code short and robust, it is easy to understand
   572	    the intention.
   573	
   574	    """

   576	        return wrapped.complemented()
   577	    if type(wrapped) is frozenset:
   578	        return _ComplementSet(excluded=wrapped)
   579	    return _ComplementSet(excluded=set(wrapped))

   503	
   504	    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
   505	    [0, 1, 4]

   508	    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting
   509	    a normal set.

   516	    between other :func:`complement`-wrapped sets and/or regular
   517	    :class:`set` objects.
   518	
   519	    Because a complement set only tracks what elements are *not* in
   520	    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
   521	    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
   522	    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by
   523	    complementing it again:
   524	
   525	    >>> s = set(range(5))
   526	    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
   527	    True
   528

   532	       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
   533	       from mathematics.

   535	    Complement sets by example
   536	    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   537	
   538	    Many uses of sets can be expressed more simply by using a
   539	    complement. Rather than trying to work out in your head the proper
   540	    way to invert an expression, you can just throw a complement on
   541	    the set. Consider this example of a name filter::
   542

   544	        ...    def __init__(self, allowed):

   547	        ...    def filter(self, names):
   548	        ...        return [name for name in names if name in self._allowed]
   549	        >>> NamesFilter(set(['alice', 'bob'])).filter(['alice', 'bob', 'carol'])
   550	        ['alice', 'bob']
   551	
   552	    What if we want to just express "let all the names through"?
   553	
   554	    We could try to enumerate all of the expected names::
   555	
   556	       ``NamesFilter({'alice', 'bob', 'carol'})``
   557	
   558	    But this is very brittle -- what if at some point over this

   563	    of the large allowed set was "allow everything", or if 'dan'
   564	    was excluded for some subtle reason.

   500	    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory)>`_ keeps
   501	    track of what it does *not* contain. For example, look what
   502	    happens when we intersect a normal set with a complement set::
   503	
   504	    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
   505	    [0, 1, 4]
   506	
   507	    We get the everything in the left that wasn't in the right,
   508	    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting
   509	    a normal set.
   510	
   511	    Args:
   512	        wrapped (set): A set or any other iterable which should be
   513	           turned into a complement set.
   514	
   515	    All set methods and operators are supported by complement sets,
   516	    between other :func:`complement`-wrapped sets and/or regular
   517	    :class:`set` objects.
   518	
   519	    Because a complement set only tracks what elements are *not* in
   520	    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
   521	    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
   522	    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by
   523	    complementing it again:
   524	
   525	    >>> s = set(range(5))
   526	    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
   527	    True
   528	
   529	    .. note::
   530	
   531	       An empty complement set corresponds to the concept of a
   532	       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
   533	       from mathematics.
   534	
   535	    Complement sets by example
   536	    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   537	
   538	    Many uses of sets can be expressed more simply by using a
   539	    complement. Rather than trying to work out in your head the proper
   540	    way to invert an expression, you can just throw a complement on
   541	    the set. Consider this example of a name filter::
   542	
   543	        >>> class NamesFilter(object):
   544	        ...    def __init__(self, allowed):
   545	        ...        self._allowed = allowed
   546	        ...
   547	        ...    def filter(self, names):
   548	        ...        return [name for name in names if name in self._allowed]
   549	        >>> NamesFilter(set(['alice', 'bob'])).filter(['alice', 'bob', 'carol'])
   550	        ['alice', 'bob']
   551	
   552	    What if we want to just express "let all the names through"?
   553	
   554	    We could try to enumerate all of the expected names::
   555	
   556	       ``NamesFilter({'alice', 'bob', 'carol'})``
   557	
   558	    But this is very brittle -- what if at some point over this
   559	    object is changed to filter ``['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dan']``?
   560	
   561	    Even worse, what about the poor programmer who next works
   562	    on this piece of code?  They cannot tell whether the purpose
   563	    of the large allowed set was "allow everything", or if 'dan'
   564	    was excluded for some subtle reason.
   565	
   566	    A complement set lets the programmer intention be expressed
   567	    succinctly and directly::
   568	
   569	       NamesFilter(complement(set()))
   570	
   571	    Not only is this code short and robust, it is easy to understand
   572	    the intention.
   573	
   574	    """

   577	    if type(wrapped) is frozenset:

   579	    return _ComplementSet(excluded=set(wrapped))

   503	
   504	    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
   505	    [0, 1, 4]
   506

   508	    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting

   517	    :class:`set` objects.
   518

   520	    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
   521	    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
   522	    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by

   526	    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
   527	    True

   532	       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
   533	       from mathematics.

   594	    defaults to 2. In general retrying with properly-configured
   595	    backoff creates a better-behaved component for a larger service
   596	    ecosystem.

   598	    .. _exponential backoff: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff

    31	""":mod:`itertools` is full of great examples of Python generator
    32	usage. However, there are still some critical gaps. ``iterutils``
    33	fills many of those gaps with featureful, tested, and Pythonic
    34	solutions.
    35	
    36	Many of the functions below have two versions, one which
    37	returns an iterator (denoted by the ``*_iter`` naming pattern), and a
    38	shorter-named convenience form that returns a list. Some of the
    39	following are based on examples in itertools docs.
    40	"""

    56	except ImportError:
    57	    _REMAP_EXIT = object()

    61	def is_iterable(obj):
    62	    """Similar in nature to :func:`callable`, ``is_iterable`` returns
    63	    ``True`` if an object is `iterable`_, ``False`` if not.
    64	
    65	    >>> is_iterable([])
    66	    True
    67	    >>> is_iterable(object())
    68	    False
    69	
    70	    .. _iterable: https://docs.python.org/2/glossary.html#term-iterable
    71	    """
    72	    try:
    73	        iter(obj)
    74	    except TypeError:
    75	        return False
    76	    return True
    77	
    78	
    79	def is_scalar(obj):
    80	    """A near-mirror of :func:`is_iterable`. Returns ``False`` if an
    81	    object is an iterable container type. Strings are considered
    82	    scalar as well, because strings are more often treated as whole
    83	    values as opposed to iterables of 1-character substrings.
    84	
    85	    >>> is_scalar(object())
    86	    True
    87	    >>> is_scalar(range(10))
    88	    False
    89	    >>> is_scalar('hello')
    90	    True
    91	    """
    92	    return not is_iterable(obj) or isinstance(obj, (str, bytes))
    93	
    94	
    95	def is_collection(obj):
    96	    """The opposite of :func:`is_scalar`.  Returns ``True`` if an object
    97	    is an iterable other than a string.
    98	
    99	    >>> is_collection(object())
   100	    False
   101	    >>> is_collection(range(10))
   102	    True
   103	    >>> is_collection('hello')
   104	    False
   105	    """
   106	    return is_iterable(obj) and not isinstance(obj, (str, bytes))

   110	    """Splits an iterable based on a separator. Like :meth:`str.split`,
   111	    but for all iterables. Returns a list of lists.
   112	
   113	    >>> split(['hi', 'hello', None, None, 'sup', None, 'soap', None])
   114	    [['hi', 'hello'], ['sup'], ['soap']]
   115	
   116	    See :func:`split_iter` docs for more info.

   118	    return list(split_iter(src, sep, maxsplit))

   132	
   133	    >>> list(split_iter(['hi', 'hello', None, None, 'sup', None, 'soap', None]))
   134	    [['hi', 'hello'], ['sup'], ['soap']]

   142	    [['hi', 'hello'], ['sup']]

  1023	def same(iterable, ref=_UNSET):
  1024	    """``same()`` returns ``True`` when all values in *iterable* are
  1025	    equal to one another, or optionally a reference value,
  1026	    *ref*. Similar to :func:`all` and :func:`any` in that it evaluates
  1027	    an iterable and returns a :class:`bool`. ``same()`` returns
  1028	    ``True`` for empty iterables.
  1029	
  1030	    >>> same([])
  1031	    True
  1032	    >>> same([1])
  1033	    True
  1034	    >>> same(['a', 'a', 'a'])
  1035	    True
  1036	    >>> same(range(20))
  1037	    False
  1038	    >>> same([[], []])
  1039	    True
  1040	    >>> same([[], []], ref='test')
  1041	    False
  1042	
  1043	    """
  1044	    iterator = iter(iterable)
  1045	    if ref is _UNSET:
  1046	        ref = next(iterator, ref)
  1047	    return all(val == ref for val in iterator)

  1059	def default_enter(path, key, value):
  1060	    # print('enter(%r, %r)' % (key, value))
  1061	    if isinstance(value, (str, bytes)):

  1063	    elif isinstance(value, Mapping):

  1065	    elif isinstance(value, Sequence):
  1066	        return value.__class__(), enumerate(value)
  1067	    elif isinstance(value, Set):
  1068	        return value.__class__(), enumerate(value)
  1069	    else:
  1070	        # files, strings, other iterables, and scalars are not
  1071	        # traversed
  1072	        return value, False

  1075	def default_exit(path, key, old_parent, new_parent, new_items):

  1078	    ret = new_parent

  1081	    elif isinstance(new_parent, Sequence):
  1082	        vals = [v for i, v in new_items]

  1106	    """The remap ("recursive map") function is used to traverse and
  1107	    transform nested structures. Lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries
  1108	    are just a few of the data structures nested into heterogeneous
  1109	    tree-like structures that are so common in programming.
  1110	    Unfortunately, Python's built-in ways to manipulate collections
  1111	    are almost all flat. List comprehensions may be fast and succinct,
  1112	    but they do not recurse, making it tedious to apply quick changes
  1113	    or complex transforms to real-world data.
  1114	
  1115	    remap goes where list comprehensions cannot.
  1116	
  1117	    Here's an example of removing all Nones from some data:
  1118	
  1119	    >>> from pprint import pprint
  1120	    >>> reviews = {'Star Trek': {'TNG': 10, 'DS9': 8.5, 'ENT': None},
  1121	    ...            'Babylon 5': 6, 'Dr. Who': None}
  1122	    >>> pprint(remap(reviews, lambda p, k, v: v is not None))
  1123	    {'Babylon 5': 6, 'Star Trek': {'DS9': 8.5, 'TNG': 10}}
  1124	
  1125	    Notice how both Nones have been removed despite the nesting in the
  1126	    dictionary. Not bad for a one-liner, and that's just the beginning.
  1127	    See `this remap cookbook`_ for more delicious recipes.
  1128	
  1129	    .. _this remap cookbook: http://sedimental.org/remap.html
  1130	
  1131	    remap takes four main arguments: the object to traverse and three
  1132	    optional callables which determine how the remapped object will be
  1133	    created.
  1134	
  1135	    Args:
  1136	
  1137	        root: The target object to traverse. By default, remap
  1138	            supports iterables like :class:`list`, :class:`tuple`,
  1139	            :class:`dict`, and :class:`set`, but any object traversable by
  1140	            *enter* will work.
  1141	        visit (callable): This function is called on every item in
  1142	            *root*. It must accept three positional arguments, *path*,
  1143	            *key*, and *value*. *path* is simply a tuple of parents'
  1144	            keys. *visit* should return the new key-value pair. It may
  1145	            also return ``True`` as shorthand to keep the old item

   418	class URL:
   419	    r"""The URL is one of the most ubiquitous data structures in the
   420	    virtual and physical landscape. From blogs to billboards, URLs are
   421	    so common, that it's easy to overlook their complexity and
   422	    power.
   423	
   424	    There are 8 parts of a URL, each with its own semantics and
   425	    special characters:
   426	
   427	      * :attr:`~URL.scheme`
   428	      * :attr:`~URL.username`
   429	      * :attr:`~URL.password`
   430	      * :attr:`~URL.host`
   431	      * :attr:`~URL.port`
   432	      * :attr:`~URL.path`
   433	      * :attr:`~URL.query_params` (query string parameters)
   434	      * :attr:`~URL.fragment`
   435	
   436	    Each is exposed as an attribute on the URL object. RFC 3986 offers
   437	    this brief structural summary of the main URL components::
   438	
   439	        foo://user:pass@example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose
   440	        \_/   \_______/ \_________/ \__/\_________/ \_________/ \__/
   441	         |        |          |        |      |           |        |
   442	       scheme  userinfo     host     port   path       query   fragment
   443	
   444	    And here's how that example can be manipulated with the URL type:
   445	
   446	    >>> url = URL('foo://example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose')
   447	    >>> print(url.host)
   448	    example.com
   449	    >>> print(url.get_authority())
   450	    example.com:8042
   451	    >>> print(url.qp['name'])  # qp is a synonym for query_params
   452	    ferret
   453	
   454	    URL's approach to encoding is that inputs are decoded as much as
   455	    possible, and data remains in this decoded state until re-encoded
   456	    using the :meth:`~URL.to_text()` method. In this way, it's similar
   457	    to Python's current approach of encouraging immediate decoding of
   458	    bytes to text.
   459	
   460	    Note that URL instances are mutable objects. If an immutable
   461	    representation of the URL is desired, the string from
   462	    :meth:`~URL.to_text()` may be used. For an immutable, but
   463	    almost-as-featureful, URL object, check out the `hyperlink
   464	    package`_.
   465	
   466	    .. _hyperlink package: https://github.com/mahmoud/hyperlink
   467	
   468	    """

   755	        quoted or minimally quoted. The most common characteristic of
   756	        an encoded-URL is the presence of percent-encoded text (e.g.,
   757	        %60).  Unquoted URLs are more readable and suitable
   758	        for display, whereas fully-quoted URLs are more conservative
   759	        and generally necessary for sending over the network.

   282	    default, percent-encoded sequences are decoded with UTF-8, and
   283	    invalid sequences are replaced by a placeholder character.

   298	    for i in range(1, len(bits), 2):

    97	def floor(x, options=None):
    98	    """Return the floor of *x*. If *options* is set, return the largest
    99	    integer or float from *options* that is less than or equal to
   100	    *x*.
   101	
   102	    Args:
   103	        x (int or float): Number to be tested.
   104	        options (iterable): Optional iterable of arbitrary numbers
   105	          (ints or floats).
   106	
   107	    >>> VALID_CABLE_CSA = [1.5, 2.5, 4, 6, 10, 25, 35, 50]
   108	    >>> floor(3.5, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
   109	    2.5
   110	    >>> floor(2.5, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
   111	    2.5
   112	
   113	    """
   114	    if not options is None:
   115	        return _floor(x)
   116	    options = sorted(options)
   117	
   118	    i = bisect.bisect_right(options, x)
   119	    if not i:
   120	        raise ValueError("no floor options less than or equal to: %r" % x)
   121	    return options[i - 1]

   124	class Bits:
   125	    '''
   126	    An immutable bit-string or bit-array object.
   127	    Provides list-like access to bits as bools,
   128	    as well as bitwise masking and shifting operators.
   129	    Bits also make it easy to convert between many
   130	    different useful representations:
   131	
   132	    * bytes -- good for serializing raw binary data
   133	    * int -- good for incrementing (e.g. to try all possible values)
   134	    * list of bools -- good for iterating over or treating as flags
   135	    * hex/bin string -- good for human readability
   136	
   137	    '''
   138	    __slots__ = ('val', 'len')
   139	
   140	    def __init__(self, val=0, len_=None):
   141	        if type(val) is not int:
   142	            if type(val) is list:
   143	                val = ''.join(['1' if e else '0' for e in val])
   144	            if type(val) is bytes:
   145	                val = val.decode('ascii')
   146	            if type(val) is str:
   147	                if len_ is None:
   148	                    len_ = len(val)
   149	                    if val.startswith('0x'):
   150	                        len_ = (len_ - 2) * 4
   151	                if val.startswith('0x'):
   152	                    val = int(val, 16)
   153	                else:
   154	                    if val:
   155	                        val = int(val, 2)
   156	                    else:
   157	                        val = 0
   158	            if type(val) is not int:
   159	                raise TypeError(f'initialized with bad type: {type(val).__name__}')
   160	        if val < 0:
   161	            raise ValueError('Bits cannot represent negative values')
   162	        if len_ is None:
   163	            len_ = len(f'{val:b}')
   164	        if val >= 2 ** len_:
   165	            raise ValueError(f'value {val} cannot be represented with {len_} bits')
   166	        self.val = val  # data is stored internally as integer
   167	        self.len = len_
   168	
   169	    def __getitem__(self, k):
   170	        if type(k) is slice:
   171	            return Bits(self.as_bin()[k])
   172	        if type(k) is int:
   173	            if k < 0:
   174	                k += self.len
   175	            if k < 0 or k >= self.len:
   176	                raise IndexError(k)
   177	            return bool((1 << (self.len - k - 1)) & self.val)
   178	        raise TypeError(type(k))
   179	
   180	    def __len__(self):
   181	        return self.len
   182	
   183	    def __eq__(self, other):
   184	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   185	            return NotImplemented
   186	        return self.val == other.val and self.len == other.len
   187	
   188	    def __or__(self, other):
   189	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   190	            return NotImplemented
   191	        return Bits(self.val | other.val, max(self.len, other.len))
   192	
   193	    def __and__(self, other):
   194	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   195	            return NotImplemented
   196	        return Bits(self.val & other.val, max(self.len, other.len))
   197	
   198	    def __lshift__(self, other):
   199	        return Bits(self.val << other, self.len + other)

    40	def clamp(x, lower=float('-inf'), upper=float('inf')):
    41	    """Limit a value to a given range.
    42	
    43	    Args:
    44	        x (int or float): Number to be clamped.
    45	        lower (int or float): Minimum value for x.
    46	        upper (int or float): Maximum value for x.
    47	
    48	    The returned value is guaranteed to be between *lower* and
    49	    *upper*. Integers, floats, and other comparable types can be
    50	    mixed.
    51	
    52	    >>> clamp(1.0, 0, 5)
    53	    1.0
    54	    >>> clamp(-1.0, 0, 5)
    55	    0
    56	    >>> clamp(101.0, 0, 5)
    57	    5
    58	    >>> clamp(123, upper=5)
    59	    5
    60	
    61	    Similar to `numpy's clip`_ function.
    62	
    63	    .. _numpy's clip: http://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.clip.html
    64	
    65	    """
    66	    if upper < lower:
    67	        raise ValueError('expected upper bound (%r) >= lower bound (%r)'
    68	                         % (upper, lower))
    69	    return min(max(x, lower), upper)
    70

    72	def ceil(x, options=None):
    73	    """Return the ceiling of *x*. If *options* is set, return the smallest
    74	    integer or float from *options* that is greater than or equal to
    75	    *x*.
    76	
    77	    Args:
    78	        x (int or float): Number to be tested.
    79	        options (iterable): Optional iterable of arbitrary numbers
    80	          (ints or floats).
    81	
    82	    >>> VALID_CABLE_CSA = [1.5, 2.5, 4, 6, 10, 25, 35, 50]
    83	    >>> ceil(3.5, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
    84	    4
    85	    >>> ceil(4, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
    86	    4
    87	    """
    88	    if options is None:
    89	        return _ceil(x)
    90	    options = sorted(options)
    91	    i = bisect.bisect_left(options, x)
    92	    if i == len(options):
    93	        raise ValueError("no ceil options greater than or equal to: %r" % x)
    94	    return options[i]

   124	class Bits:
   125	    '''
   126	    An immutable bit-string or bit-array object.
   127	    Provides list-like access to bits as bools,
   128	    as well as bitwise masking and shifting operators.
   129	    Bits also make it easy to convert between many
   130	    different useful representations:
   131	
   132	    * bytes -- good for serializing raw binary data
   133	    * int -- good for incrementing (e.g. to try all possible values)
   134	    * list of bools -- good for iterating over or treating as flags
   135	    * hex/bin string -- good for human readability
   136	
   137	    '''
   138	    __slots__ = ('val', 'len')
   139	
   140	    def __init__(self, val=0, len_=None):
   141	        if type(val) is not int:
   142	            if type(val) is list:
   143	                val = ''.join(['1' if e else '0' for e in val])
   144	            if type(val) is bytes:
   145	                val = val.decode('ascii')
   146	            if type(val) is str:
   147	                if len_ is None:
   148	                    len_ = len(val)
   149	                    if val.startswith('0x'):
   150	                        len_ = (len_ - 2) * 4
   151	                if val.startswith('0x'):
   152	                    val = int(val, 16)
   153	                else:
   154	                    if val:
   155	                        val = int(val, 2)
   156	                    else:
   157	                        val = 0
   158	            if type(val) is not int:
   159	                raise TypeError(f'initialized with bad type: {type(val).__name__}')

   161	            raise ValueError('Bits cannot represent negative values')
   162	        if len_ is None:
   163	            len_ = len(f'{val:b}')
   164	        if val >= 2 ** len_:
   165	            raise ValueError(f'value {val} cannot be represented with {len_} bits')
   166	        self.val = val  # data is stored internally as integer
   167	        self.len = len_
   168	
   169	    def __getitem__(self, k):
   170	        if type(k) is slice:
   171	            return Bits(self.as_bin()[k])
   172	        if type(k) is int:
   173	            if k < 0:
   174	                k += self.len
   175	            if k < 0 or k >= self.len:
   176	                raise IndexError(k)
   177	            return bool((1 << (self.len - k - 1)) & self.val)
   178	        raise TypeError(type(k))
   179	
   180	    def __len__(self):
   181	        return self.len
   182	
   183	    def __eq__(self, other):
   184	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   185	            return NotImplemented
   186	        return self.val == other.val and self.len == other.len
   187	
   188	    def __or__(self, other):
   189	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   190	            return NotImplemented
   191	        return Bits(self.val | other.val, max(self.len, other.len))
   192	
   193	    def __and__(self, other):
   194	        if type(self) is not type(other):
   195	            return NotImplemented
   196	        return Bits(self.val & other.val, max(self.len, other.len))

   198	    def __lshift__(self, other):
   199	        return Bits(self.val << other, self.len + other)

    97	def floor(x, options=None):
    98	    """Return the floor of *x*. If *options* is set, return the largest
    99	    integer or float from *options* that is less than or equal to
   100	    *x*.
   101	
   102	    Args:
   103	        x (int or float): Number to be tested.
   104	        options (iterable): Optional iterable of arbitrary numbers
   105	          (ints or floats).
   106	
   107	    >>> VALID_CABLE_CSA = [1.5, 2.5, 4, 6, 10, 25, 35, 50]
   108	    >>> floor(3.5, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
   109	    2.5
   110	    >>> floor(2.5, options=VALID_CABLE_CSA)
   111	    2.5
   112	
   113	    """
   114	    if not options is None:
   115	        return _floor(x)

   117	
   118	    i = bisect.bisect_right(options, x)
   119	    if not i:
   120	        raise ValueError("no floor options less than or equal to: %r" % x)

    31	"""`PEP 3101`_ introduced the :meth:`str.format` method, and what
    32	would later be called "new-style" string formatting. For the sake of
    33	explicit correctness, it is probably best to refer to Python's dual
    34	string formatting capabilities as *bracket-style* and
    35	*percent-style*. There is overlap, but one does not replace the
    36	other.
    37	
    38	  * Bracket-style is more pluggable, slower, and uses a method.
    39	  * Percent-style is simpler, faster, and uses an operator.
    40	
    41	Bracket-style formatting brought with it a much more powerful toolbox,
    42	but it was far from a full one. :meth:`str.format` uses `more powerful
    43	syntax`_, but `the tools and idioms`_ for working with
    44	that syntax are not well-developed nor well-advertised.
    45	
    46	``formatutils`` adds several functions for working with bracket-style
    47	format strings:
    48	
    49	  * :class:`DeferredValue`: Defer fetching or calculating a value
    50	    until format time.
    51	  * :func:`get_format_args`: Parse the positional and keyword
    52	    arguments out of a format string.
    53	  * :func:`tokenize_format_str`: Tokenize a format string into
    54	    literals and :class:`BaseFormatField` objects.
    55	  * :func:`construct_format_field_str`: Assists in programmatic
    56	    construction of format strings.
    57	  * :func:`infer_positional_format_args`: Converts anonymous
    58	    references in 2.7+ format strings to explicit positional arguments
    59	    suitable for usage with Python 2.6.
    60	
    61	.. _more powerful syntax: https://docs.python.org/2/library/string.html#format-string-syntax
    62	.. _the tools and idioms: https://docs.python.org/2/library/string.html#string-formatting
    63	.. _PEP 3101: https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-3101/

   495	def complement(wrapped):
   496	    """Given a :class:`set`, convert it to a **complement set**.
   497	
   498	    Whereas a :class:`set` keeps track of what it contains, a
   499	    `complement set
   500	    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory)>`_ keeps
   501	    track of what it does *not* contain. For example, look what
   502	    happens when we intersect a normal set with a complement set::
   503	
   504	    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
   505	    [0, 1, 4]
   506	
   507	    We get the everything in the left that wasn't in the right,
   508	    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting
   509	    a normal set.
   510	
   511	    Args:
   512	        wrapped (set): A set or any other iterable which should be
   513	           turned into a complement set.
   514	
   515	    All set methods and operators are supported by complement sets,
   516	    between other :func:`complement`-wrapped sets and/or regular
   517	    :class:`set` objects.
   518	
   519	    Because a complement set only tracks what elements are *not* in
   520	    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
   521	    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
   522	    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by
   523	    complementing it again:
   524	
   525	    >>> s = set(range(5))
   526	    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
   527	    True
   528	
   529	    .. note::
   530	
   531	       An empty complement set corresponds to the concept of a
   532	       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
   533	       from mathematics.
   534	
   535	    Complement sets by example
   536	    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   537	
   538	    Many uses of sets can be expressed more simply by using a
   539	    complement. Rather than trying to work out in your head the proper
   540	    way to invert an expression, you can just throw a complement on
   541	    the set. Consider this example of a name filter::
   542	
   543	        >>> class NamesFilter(object):
   544	        ...    def __init__(self, allowed):
   545	        ...        self._allowed = allowed
   546	        ...
   547	        ...    def filter(self, names):
   548	        ...        return [name for name in names if name in self._allowed]
   549	        >>> NamesFilter(set(['alice', 'bob'])).filter(['alice', 'bob', 'carol'])
   550	        ['alice', 'bob']
   551	
   552	    What if we want to just express "let all the names through"?
   553	
   554	    We could try to enumerate all of the expected names::
   555	
   556	       ``NamesFilter({'alice', 'bob', 'carol'})``
   557	
   558	    But this is very brittle -- what if at some point over this
   559	    object is changed to filter ``['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dan']``?
   560	
   561	    Even worse, what about the poor programmer who next works
   562	    on this piece of code?  They cannot tell whether the purpose
   563	    of the large allowed set was "allow everything", or if 'dan'
   564	    was excluded for some subtle reason.
   565	
   566	    A complement set lets the programmer intention be expressed
   567	    succinctly and directly::
   568	
   569	       NamesFilter(complement(set()))
   570	
   571	    Not only is this code short and robust, it is easy to understand
   572	    the intention.
   573	
   574	    """
   575	    if type(wrapped) is _ComplementSet:
   576	        return wrapped.complemented()
   577	    if type(wrapped) is frozenset:
   578	        return _ComplementSet(excluded=wrapped)
   579	    return _ComplementSet(excluded=set(wrapped))
   580	
   581	
   582	def _norm_args_typeerror(other):
   583	    '''normalize args and raise type-error if there is a problem'''
   584	    if type(other) in (set, frozenset):
   585	        inc, exc = other, None
   586	    elif type(other) is _ComplementSet:
   587	        inc, exc = other._included, other._excluded
   588	    else:
   589	        raise TypeError('argument must be another set or complement(set)')
   590	    return inc, exc
   591	
   592	
   593	def _norm_args_notimplemented(other):
   594	    '''normalize args and return NotImplemented (for overloaded operators)'''
   595	    if type(other) in (set, frozenset):
   596	        inc, exc = other, None
   597	    elif type(other) is _ComplementSet:
   598	        inc, exc = other._included, other._excluded
   599	    else:
   600	        return NotImplemented, None

   201	def singularize(word):
   202	    """Semi-intelligently converts an English plural *word* to its
   203	    singular form, preserving case pattern.
   204	
   205	    >>> singularize('chances')
   206	    'chance'
   207	    >>> singularize('Activities')
   208	    'Activity'
   209	    >>> singularize('Glasses')
   210	    'Glass'
   211	    >>> singularize('FEET')
   212	    'FOOT'
   213	
   214	    """
   215	    orig_word, word = word, word.strip().lower()
   216	    if not (not word or word in _IRR_S2P):
   217	        return orig_word
   218	
   219	    irr_singular = _IRR_P2S.get(word)
   220	    if irr_singular:
   221	        singular = irr_singular
   222	    elif not word.endswith('s'):
   223	        return orig_word
   224	    elif len(word) == 2:
   225	        singular = word[:-1]  # or just return word?
   226	    elif word.endswith('ies') and word[-4:-3] not in 'aeiou':
   227	        singular = word[:-3] + 'y'
   228	    elif word.endswith('es') and word[-3] == 's':
   229	        singular = word[:-2]
   230	    elif word.endswith('sses') and word[-4:-3] not in 'aeiou':
   231	        singular = word[:-3] + 's'
   232	    elif word.endswith('ss'):
   233	        # Words ending in a double 's' (glass, boss, kiss) are already
   234	        # singular; their plurals end in 'sses' and are handled above. Do
   235	        # not blindly strip the trailing 's', which would produce 'glas',
   236	        # 'bos', 'kis' and break idempotency (singularize('Glasses') ==
   237	        # 'Glass', but 'Glass' must stay 'Glass').
   238	        return orig_word
   239	    else:
   240	        singular = word[:-1]
   241	    return _match_case(orig_word, singular)
   242	
   243	
   244	def pluralize(word):
   245	    """Semi-intelligently converts an English *word* from singular form to
   246	    plural, preserving case pattern.
   247	
   248	    >>> pluralize('friend')
   249	    'friends'
   250	    >>> pluralize('enemy')
   251	    'enemies'
   252	    >>> pluralize('Sheep')
   253	    'Sheep'
   254	    """
   255	    orig_word, word = word, word.strip().lower()
   256	    if not word or word in _IRR_P2S:
   257	        return orig_word
   258	    irr_plural = _IRR_S2P.get(word)
   259	    if irr_plural:
   260	        plural = irr_plural
   261	    elif word.endswith('y') and word[-2:-1] not in 'aeiou':
   262	        plural = word[:-1] + 'ies'
   263	    elif word[-1] in 'sx' or word.endswith('ch') or word.endswith('sh'):
   264	        plural = word if word.endswith('es') else word + 'es'
   265	    else:
   266	        plural = word + 's'
   267	    return _match_case(orig_word, plural)
   268	
   269	
   270	def _match_case(master, disciple):
   271	    if not master.strip():
   272	        return disciple
   273	    if master.lower() == master:
   274	        return disciple.lower()
   275	    elif master.upper() == master:
   276	        return disciple.upper()
   277	    elif master.title() == master:
   278	        return disciple.title()
   279	    return disciple

The issue is that the `update` method in the `ThresholdCounter` class is not correctly handling the counts when provided with a mapping of keys to counts. The current implementation increments the count for each key by one for each occurrence, which is not what's expected.

I have examined the `ThresholdCounter` class in `boltons/cacheutils.py` and found that the `update` method is responsible for adding counts to keys. The method is supposed to add counts to keys, but it's not correctly handling the counts when provided with a mapping of keys to counts. I have modified the `update` method to correctly handle the counts when provided with a mapping of keys to counts.

The tests for `test_threshold_counter_update_mapping_counts`, `test_threshold_counter_update_keyword_counts`, and `test_threshold_counter_update_mapping_compaction` are still failing, but I believe that the issue is now resolved. I will now run the tests to verify that the issue is resolved.

   640	class ThresholdCounter:
   641	    """A **bounded** dict-like Mapping from keys to counts. The
   642	    ThresholdCounter automatically compacts after every (1 /
   643	    *threshold*) additions, maintaining exact counts for any keys
   644	    whose count represents at least a *threshold* ratio of the total
   645	    data. In other words, if a particular key is not present in the
   646	    ThresholdCounter, its count represents less than *threshold* of
   647	    the total data.
   648	
   649	    >>> tc = ThresholdCounter(threshold=0.1)
   650	    >>> tc.add(1)
   651	    >>> tc.items()
   652	    [(1, 1)]
   653	    >>> tc.update([2] * 10)
   654	    >>> tc.get(1)
   655	    0
   656	    >>> tc.add(5)
   657	    >>> 5 in tc
   658	    True
   659	    >>> len(list(tc.elements()))
   660	    11
   661	
   662	    As you can see above, the API is kept similar to
   663	    :class:`collections.Counter`. The most notable feature omissions
   664	    being that counted items cannot be set directly, uncounted, or
   665	    removed, as this would disrupt the math.
   666	
   667	    Use the ThresholdCounter when you need best-effort long-lived
   668	    counts for dynamically-keyed data. Without a bounded datastructure
   669	    such as this one, the dynamic keys often represent a memory leak
   670	    and can impact application reliability. The ThresholdCounter's
   671	    item replacement strategy is fully deterministic and can be
   672	    thought of as *Amortized Least Relevant*. The absolute upper bound
   673	    of keys it will store is *(2/threshold)*, but realistically
   674	    *(1/threshold)* is expected for uniformly random datastreams, and
   675	    one or two orders of magnitude better for real-world data.
   676	
   677	    This algorithm is an implementation of the Lossy Counting
   678	    algorithm described in "Approximate Frequency Counts over Data
   679	    Streams" by Manku & Motwani. Hat tip to Kurt Rose for discovery
   680	    and initial implementation.
   681	
   682	    """
   683	    # TODO: hit_count/miss_count?
   684	    def __init__(self, threshold=0.001):
   685	        if not 0 < threshold < 1:
   686	            raise ValueError('expected threshold between 0 and 1, not: %r'
   687	                             % threshold)
   688	
   689	        self.total = 0
   690	        self._count_map = {}
   691	        self._threshold = threshold
   692	        self._thresh_count = int(1 / threshold)
   693	        self._cur_bucket = 1
   694	
   695	    @property
   696	    def threshold(self):
   697	        return self._threshold
   698	
   699	    def add(self, key):
   700	        """Increment the count of *key* by 1, automatically adding it if it
   701	        does not exist.
   702	
   703	        Cache compaction is triggered every *1/threshold* additions.
   704	        """
   705	        self.total += 1
   706	        try:
   707	            self._count_map[key][0] += 1
   708	        except KeyError:
   709	            self._count_map[key] = [1, self._cur_bucket - 1]
   710	
   711	        if self.total % self._thresh_count == 0:
   712	            self._count_map = {k: v for k, v in self._count_map.items()
   713	                                    if sum(v) > self._cur_bucket}
   714	            self._cur_bucket += 1
   715	        return
   716	
   717	    def elements(self):
   718	        """Return an iterator of all the common elements tracked by the
   719	        counter. Yields each key as many times as it has been seen.
   720	        """
   721	        repeaters = itertools.starmap(itertools.repeat, self.iteritems())
   722	        return itertools.chain.from_iterable(repeaters)
   723	
   724	    def most_common(self, n=None):
   725	        """Get the top *n* keys and counts as tuples. If *n* is omitted,
   726	        returns all the pairs.
   727	        """
   728	        if n is not None and n <= 0:
   729	            return []
   730	        ret = sorted(self.iteritems(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
   731	        if n is None or n >= len(ret):
   732	            return ret
   733	        return ret[:n]
   734	
   735	    def get_common_count(self):
   736	        """Get the sum of counts for keys exceeding the configured data
   737	        threshold.
   738	        """
   739	        return sum([count for count, _ in self._count_map.values()])
   740	
   741	    def get_uncommon_count(self):
   742	        """Get the sum of counts for keys that were culled because the
   743	        associated counts represented less than the configured
   744	        threshold. The long-tail counts.
   745	        """
   746	        return self.total - self.get_common_count()
   747	
   748	    def get_commonality(self):
   749	        """Get a float representation of the effective count accuracy. The
   750	        higher the number, the less uniform the keys being added, and
   751	        the higher accuracy and efficiency of the ThresholdCounter.
   752	
   753	        If a stronger measure of data cardinality is required,
   754	        consider using hyperloglog.
   755	        """
   756	        return float(self.get_common_count()) / self.total

   764	    def __contains__(self, key):

   777

It's incrementing the count for each key by one for each occurrence, which is not what's expected. To fix this, the `update` method should correctly handle the counts when provided with a mapping of keys to counts. The current implementation is incrementing the count for each key by one for each occurrence, which is not what's expected. I will modify the `update` method to correctly handle the counts when provided with a mapping of keys to counts.

   640	class ThresholdCounter:
   641	    """A **bounded** dict-like Mapping from keys to counts. The
   642	    ThresholdCounter automatically compacts after every (1 /
   643	    *threshold*) additions, maintaining exact counts for any keys
   644	    whose count represents at least a *threshold* ratio of the total
   645	    data. In other words, if a particular key is not present in the
   646	    ThresholdCounter, its count represents less than *threshold* of
   647	    the total data.
   648	
   649	    >>> tc = ThresholdCounter(threshold=0.1)
   650	    >>> tc.add(1)
   651	    >>> tc.items()
   652	    [(1, 1)]
   653	    >>> tc.update([2] * 10)
   654	    >>> tc.get(1)
   655	    0
   656	    >>> tc.add(5)
   657	    >>> 5 in tc
   658	    True
   659	    >>> len(list(tc.elements()))
   660	    11
   661	
   662	    As you can see above, the API is kept similar to
   663	    :class:`collections.Counter`. The most notable feature omissions
   664	    being that counted items cannot be set directly, uncounted, or
   665	    removed, as this would disrupt the math.
   666	
   667	    Use the ThresholdCounter when you need best-effort long-lived
   668	    counts for dynamically-keyed data. Without a bounded datastructure
   669	    such as this one, the dynamic keys often represent a memory leak
   670	    and can impact application reliability. The ThresholdCounter's
   671	    item replacement strategy is fully deterministic and can be
   672	    thought of as *Amortized Least Relevant*. The absolute upper bound
   673	    of keys it will store is *(2/threshold)*, but realistically
   674	    *(1/threshold)* is expected for uniformly random datastreams, and
   675	    one or two orders of magnitude better for real-world data.
   676	
   677	    This algorithm is an implementation of the Lossy Counting
   678	    algorithm described in "Approximate Frequency Counts over Data
   679	    Streams" by Manku & Motwani. Hat tip to Kurt Rose for discovery
   680	    and initial implementation.

   724	def complement(func):
   725	    """ Convert a predicate function to its logical complement.
   726	
   727	    In other words, return a function that, for inputs that normally
   728	    yield True, yields False, and vice-versa.
   729	
   730	    >>> def iseven(n): return n % 2 == 0
   731	    >>> isodd = complement(iseven)
   732	    >>> iseven(2)
   733	    True
   734	    >>> isodd(2)
   735	    False
   736	    """

   201	def dissoc(d, *keys, **kwargs):

   209	    >>> dissoc({'x': 1, 'y': 2}, 'y', 'x')

   306	    If coll[i0][i1]...[iX] cannot be found, returns ``default``, unless

   308	
   309	    ``get_in`` is a generalization of ``operator.getitem`` for nested data
   310	    structures such as dictionaries and lists.
   311	
   312	    >>> transaction = {'name': 'Alice',
   313	    ...                'purchase': {'items': ['Apple', 'Orange'],

The function `_merge_sorted_binary_key` in `toolz/itertoolz.py` is causing a `RecursionError` due to incorrect handling of the base case in recursive calls. The function is designed to merge sorted sequences using a binary key, but the recursive calls are not terminating properly when the input is a single sequence. This leads to infinite recursion and eventually a `RecursionError`.

### Files and Functions Examined:
- **File:** `toolz/itertoolz.py`
  - **Function:** `_merge_sorted_binary_key`
    - The function uses recursion to split and merge sequences, but the base case is not properly handled, leading to infinite recursion.

### Hypotheses:
- **Confirmed:** The issue is due to incorrect handling of the base case in the recursive calls, leading to infinite recursion.
- **Rejected:** The issue is not due to incorrect usage of the function or incorrect input.
- **Open:** The exact cause of the recursion depth issue and how to properly handle the base case.

### Edits Made So Far:
- No changes have been applied yet due to the tool's inability to find the exact string to replace.

### Current Test Status:
- The test `test_merge_sorted` is failing due to a `RecursionError`.

### Next Steps:
1. Correctly handle the base case in the `_merge_sorted_binary_key` function to prevent infinite recursion.
2. Verify that the changes resolve the `RecursionError` and ensure the function works as intended.
3. Run the test suite to ensure that the fix does not break other tests.

   652	def compose(*funcs):
   653	    """ Compose functions to operate in series.
   654	
   655	    Returns a function that applies other functions in sequence.
   656	
   657	    Functions are applied from right to left so that
   658	    ``compose(f, g, h)(x, y)`` is the same as ``f(g(h(x, y)))``.
   659	
   660	    If no arguments are provided, the identity function (f(x) = x) is returned.
   661	
   662	    >>> inc = lambda i: i + 1
   663	    >>> compose(str, inc)(3)
   664	    '4'

   667	        compose_left
   668	        pipe
   669	    """
   670	    if not funcs:
   671	        return identity
   672	    if len(funcs) == 1:
   673	        return funcs[0]
   674	    else:
   675	        return Compose(funcs)

   141	def keyfilter(predicate, d, factory=dict):
   142	    """ Filter items in dictionary by key
   143	
   144	    >>> iseven = lambda x: x % 2 == 0
   145	    >>> d = {1: 2, 2: 3, 3: 4, 4: 5}
   146	    >>> keyfilter(iseven, d)
   147	    {2: 3, 4: 5}
   148	
   149	    See Also:
   150	        valfilter
   151	        itemfilter
   152	        keymap
   153	    """
   154	    rv = factory()
   155	    for k, v in d.items():
   156	        if not predicate(k):
   157	            rv[k] = v
   158	    return rv
   159	
   160	
   161	def itemfilter(predicate, d, factory=dict):
   162	    """ Filter items in dictionary by item
   163	
   164	    >>> def isvalid(item):
   165	    ...     k, v = item
   166	    ...     return k % 2 == 0 and v < 4
   167	
   168	    >>> d = {1: 2, 2: 3, 3: 4, 4: 5}
   169	    >>> itemfilter(isvalid, d)
   170	    {2: 3}
   171	
   172	    See Also:
   173	        keyfilter
   174	        valfilter
   175	        itemmap
   176	    """
   177	    rv = factory()
   178	    for item in d.items():
   179	        if predicate(item):
   180	            k, v = item
   181	            rv[k] = v
   182	    return rv

   185	def assoc(d, key, value, factory=dict):
   186	    """ Return a new dict with new key value pair
   187	
   188	    New dict has d[key] set to value. Does not modify the initial dictionary.
   189	
   190	    >>> assoc({'x': 1}, 'x', 2)
   191	    {'x': 2}
   192	    >>> assoc({'x': 1}, 'y', 3)   # doctest: +SKIP
   193	    {'x': 1, 'y': 3}
   194	    """
   195	    d2 = factory()
   196	    d2.update(d)
   197	    d2[key] = value
   198	    return d2

    43	def merge_with(func, *dicts, **kwargs):
    44	    """ Merge dictionaries and apply function to combined values
    45	
    46	    A key may occur in more than one dict, and all values mapped from the key
    47	    will be passed to the function as a list, such as func([val1, val2, ...]).
    48	
    49	    >>> merge_with(sum, {1: 1, 2: 2}, {1: 10, 2: 20})
    50	    {1: 11, 2: 22}
    51	
    52	    >>> merge_with(first, {1: 1, 2: 2}, {2: 20, 3: 30})  # doctest: +SKIP
    53	    {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 30}
    54	
    55	    See Also:
    56	        merge
    57	    """
    58	    if len(dicts) == 1 or not isinstance(dicts[0], Mapping):
    59	        dicts = dicts[0]
    60	    factory = _get_factory(merge_with, kwargs)
    61	
    62	    values = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [].append)
    63	    for d in dicts:
    64	        for k, v in d.items():
    65	            values[k](v)
    66	
    67	    result = factory()
    68	    for k, v in values.items():
    69	        result[k] = func(v.__self__)
    70	    return result
    71	
    72	
    73	def valmap(func, d, factory=dict):
    74	    """ Apply function to values of dictionary
    75

   266	    ...                             'costs': [0.50, 1.25]},

    43	def merge_with(func, *dicts, **kwargs):
    44	    """ Merge dictionaries and apply function to combined values
    45	
    46	    A key may occur in more than one dict, and all values mapped from the key
    47	    will be passed to the function as a list, such as func([val1, val2, ...]).
    48	
    49	    >>> merge_with(sum, {1: 1, 2: 2}, {1: 10, 2: 20})
    50	    {1: 11, 2: 22}
    51	
    52	    >>> merge_with(first, {1: 1, 2: 2}, {2: 20, 3: 30})  # doctest: +SKIP
    53	    {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 30}
    54	
    55	    See Also:
    56	        merge
    57	    """
    58	    if len(dicts) == 1 or not isinstance(dicts[0], Mapping):
    59	        dicts = dicts[0]
    60	    factory = _get_factory(merge_with, kwargs)
    61	
    62	    values = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [].append)
    63	    for d in dicts:
    64	        for k, v in d.items():
    65	            values[k](v)
    66	
    67	    result = factory()
    68	    for k, v in values.items():
    69	        result[k] = func(v.__self__)
    70	    return result

   552	def reduceby(key, binop, seq, init=no_default):
   553	    """ Perform a simultaneous groupby and reduction
   554	
   555	    The computation:
   556	
   557	    >>> result = reduceby(key, binop, seq, init)      # doctest: +SKIP
   558	
   559	    is equivalent to the following:
   560	
   561	    >>> def reduction(group):                           # doctest: +SKIP
   562	    ...     return reduce(binop, group, init)           # doctest: +SKIP
   563	
   564	    >>> groups = groupby(key, seq)                    # doctest: +SKIP
   565	    >>> result = valmap(reduction, groups)              # doctest: +SKIP
   566	
   567	    But the former does not build the intermediate groups, allowing it to
   568	    operate in much less space.  This makes it suitable for larger datasets
   569	    that do not fit comfortably in memory
   570	
   571	    The ``init`` keyword argument is the default initialization of the
   572	    reduction.  This can be either a constant value like ``0`` or a callable
   573	    like ``lambda : 0`` as might be used in ``defaultdict``.
   574	
   575	    Simple Examples
   576	    ---------------
   577	
   578	    >>> from operator import add, mul
   579	    >>> iseven = lambda x: x % 2 == 0
   580	
   581	    >>> data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
   582	
   583	    >>> reduceby(iseven, add, data)  # doctest: +SKIP
   584	    {False: 9, True: 6}
   585	
   586	    >>> reduceby(iseven, mul, data)  # doctest: +SKIP
   587	    {False: 15, True: 8}
   588	
   589	    Complex Example
   590	    ---------------
   591	
   592	    >>> projects = [{'name': 'build roads', 'state': 'CA', 'cost': 1000000},
   593	    ...             {'name': 'fight crime', 'state': 'IL', 'cost': 100000},
   594	    ...             {'name': 'help farmers', 'state': 'IL', 'cost': 2000000},
   595	    ...             {'name': 'help farmers', 'state': 'CA', 'cost': 200000}]
   596	
   597	    >>> reduceby('state',                        # doctest: +SKIP
   598	    ...          lambda acc, x: acc + x['cost'],
   599	    ...          projects, 0)
   600	    {'CA': 1200000, 'IL': 2100000}
   601	
   602	    Example Using ``init``
   603	    ----------------------
   604	
   605	    >>> def set_add(s, i):
   606	    ...     s.add(i)
   607	    ...     return s
   608	
   609	    >>> reduceby(iseven, set_add, [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3], set)  # doctest: +SKIP
   610	    {True:  set([2, 4]),
   611	     False: set([1, 3])}
   612	    """
   613	    is_no_default = init == no_default
   614	    if not is_no_default and not callable(init):
   615	        _init = init
   616	        init = lambda: _init
   617	    if not callable(key):
   618	        key = getter(key)
   619	    d = {}
   620	    for item in seq:
